cues.en: Welcome to Class 2: bonding, structure and properties.
In Class 1 we counted the particles in atoms and ions. Today we ask how atoms hold together, and why that decides whether a material carries current.
By the end, you will be able to choose a material for each job in a chip and support the choice with a number.
If you are studying on your own, the narration takes about fourteen minutes. Stop at the activity and at each check, then do Lab 2.
Here is the plan for today.
A five minute activity reviews Class 1.
Part one is about bonding: how different materials resist current, the three bonding models, and electronegativity. It ends with Check 1.
Part two is about structure and choice: crystalline and amorphous solids, unit cells, the resistance of a copper wire, and choosing materials. It ends with Check 2.
Then you do Lab 2 for thirty minutes, and finish with the Exit Ticket.
Activity 1. Answer four questions about Class 1 without notes, then compare with a partner.
Count the electrons in the copper two plus ion. Explain the difference between an element and a compound. Find the charge of copper in copper one oxide.
And say which particles carry the current in a copper wire.
Pause the narration now, write your answers, and then press Show answers.
By the end of today you can do six things.
Describe metallic, covalent and ionic bonding, and say which electrons can move in each.
Use electronegativity differences to classify a bond.
Explain why a bonding label alone cannot predict conduction.
Tell crystalline from amorphous structures, and count the atoms in a cubic unit cell.
Calculate the resistance of a wire, and choose silicon, copper and silicon dioxide for their jobs, with a number for each choice.
Today builds directly on Class 1.
We learned that atoms gain or lose electrons to form ions. Today we see that in an ionic solid the ions are held in place, so they cannot carry current.
We learned that silicon, copper and silicon dioxide do three jobs in a chip. Today we see that their bonding and structure explain those jobs.
A few new symbols. Rho is the electrical resistivity, in ohm meters. R is resistance in ohms, L is length, and A is the cross-sectional area. Delta chi is the electronegativity difference.
Start with the design question: why does a chip need three different materials?
Resistivity measures how strongly a material resists current, independent of its shape. The chart uses a log scale, so each grid line is a factor of one thousand.
Copper, aluminum and tungsten are near ten to the minus eight ohm meters. Pure silicon is near two thousand. Amorphous silicon dioxide is near ten to the sixteen.
So silicon dioxide resists current about ten to the power twenty three point eight times more than copper. That is a range of almost twenty four orders of magnitude.
No single material can be the wire, the switch and the insulator. A chip needs all three.
Why are these materials so different? The answer is where the electrons are.
In metallic bonding, as in copper, each atom gives about one electron to the whole solid. The ion cores sit in a sea of shared electrons, and those electrons can move.
In a covalent network, as in silicon, electrons are shared in pairs between neighboring atoms. Each pair is fixed in its bond.
In ionic bonding, as in sodium chloride, the metal gives electrons to the nonmetal. The ions are held in place by attraction between positive and negative charges.
So metals conduct. Covalent solids usually conduct poorly. Solid ionic compounds do not conduct, but when they melt or dissolve, the ions can move and they do.
These are models. Real bonds lie on a range between them.
Electronegativity, written chi, measures how strongly an atom pulls shared electrons toward itself. Oxygen pulls hard, at three point five. Sodium pulls weakly, at zero point nine.
The difference between two atoms sorts the bond. Below zero point four, the electrons are shared about equally: a nonpolar covalent bond.
From zero point four to one point eight, they are shared unequally: a polar covalent bond. Above one point eight, one atom takes the electrons: an ionic bond.
Try silicon and oxygen. The difference is three point five minus one point eight, which is one point seven. The bond is polar covalent, not ionic.
Silicon dioxide is a covalent network with partial charges.
Sodium and chlorine give two point one: ionic. Copper with copper gives zero, but two metals bond metallically, so this rule does not apply.
This is a guide with exceptions, as your textbook says. Press D to see the same rule in Python.
Now connect bonding to conduction.
In copper, the shared electrons are not tied to any one atom. When a voltage is applied, they drift together, and that drift is the current in a wire.
In silicon dioxide, every electron is held in a bond or on an atom. Freeing one takes a lot of energy, so almost none can move.
Silicon is in between. A few electrons are freed at room temperature, and doping adds more on purpose. Class 6 explains this with energy bands.
The worked example asks you to choose a material for an interconnect and for the layer between interconnects.
Copper, with a resistivity of one point six eight times ten to the minus eight, is the wire. Silicon dioxide, near ten to the sixteen, is the layer.
Here is a rule that many students propose: a covalently bonded material can never conduct.
Test it against the evidence. Graphite is covalent within its layers, and it conducts, at about ten to the minus five ohm meters along the layers.
In each layer, one electron per carbon atom is shared across the whole sheet.
Silicon is a covalent network and a semiconductor.
So the bonding label is a start, not the answer. What matters is whether some electrons are free to move. Check a property table before you decide.
Check 1. Answer these four questions on your own, in about five minutes.
Classify the sodium chlorine bond. Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct. Say which electrons carry the current in copper. And decide whether the silicon oxygen bond is ionic.
Pause now, write your answers, and then press Show answers.
Part 2 is about structure.
In a crystal, atoms sit in a pattern that repeats in every direction. Copper, silicon wafers and quartz are crystals.
In an amorphous solid, each atom has similar neighbors, but there is no repeat over long distances. The silicon dioxide grown or deposited on a chip is amorphous, like glass.
Move the slider and watch the pattern fade. There is no single point where it stops being a crystal.
Structure changes properties.
Quartz and fused silica are both silicon dioxide, with the same silicon oxygen bonds, but fused silica is about seventeen percent less dense, because its irregular network packs less well.
A unit cell is the smallest box that, repeated, builds the whole crystal.
Atoms on the corners and faces are shared with neighboring cells. A corner atom is shared by eight cells, so it counts one eighth. A face atom counts one half. An atom inside counts one.
Copper is face centered cubic: eight corners times one eighth, plus six faces times one half, gives four atoms per cell.
Silicon has the diamond structure: the same four, plus four atoms inside, gives eight.
In Class 3, these counts, with the atomic mass from Class 1, link the mass of a wafer to its number of atoms.
How much does a chip wire resist? Resistance depends on the material and the shape: R equals rho times L divided by A.
Take a copper wire one millimeter long, one hundred nanometers wide and two hundred nanometers thick.
The area is two times ten to the minus fourteen square meters, and the resistance is eight hundred forty ohms.
Switch to aluminum. The same wire resists one thousand three hundred twenty five ohms, about one point six times more. Tungsten gives two thousand eight hundred ohms.
Now halve the width. The area halves, so the resistance doubles.
This is why chip wiring moved from aluminum to copper from the late nineteen nineties.
Tungsten is still used for the short contacts that touch the transistors, because it fills narrow holes well, and because copper must be kept away from silicon.
Now the insulator. How little current crosses one hundred nanometers of silicon dioxide?
Under a pad one micrometer by one micrometer, the resistance is rho times thickness over area, about ten to the twenty one ohms.
With one volt across it, the current is about ten to the minus twenty one amperes.
That is roughly one electron every three minutes. Between two wires, silicon dioxide stops the current almost completely.
Very thin oxides, only a few nanometers, behave differently, because electrons can tunnel through them. That belongs to later courses.
Put it together. Each chip material is chosen for a number.
Copper for the wires and vias, because its resistivity is the lowest of the three metals.
Tungsten for the contacts, even though it resists more, because it fills narrow contact holes and keeps copper away from silicon.
Silicon for the transistors, because its resistivity sits in between and can be tuned by doping.
And silicon dioxide for insulation, near ten to the sixteen ohm meters.
A complete choice also weighs process steps, cost and reliability. The second half of the course returns to copper wiring in detail.

Here is a summary of today.
In metallic bonding, electrons are shared by the whole solid, so metals conduct. In covalent and ionic solids, electrons or ions are held in place, so they conduct poorly.
The electronegativity difference sorts bonds: silicon oxygen, at one point seven, is polar covalent; sodium chlorine, at two point one, is ionic.
A bonding label does not settle conduction: graphite conducts, and silicon is a semiconductor.
Crystals repeat and amorphous solids do not, and the same silicon dioxide differs in density.
And R equals rho L over A: choose the material by its resistivity, then size the wire. A one millimeter copper wire, one hundred by two hundred nanometers, has eight hundred forty ohms.
